articles.title: “It’s Not a Comeback Story”: Former Browns QB Stands Against Deshaun Watson’s Redemption Arc Despite 3–1 Start
articles.summary: Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders quarterback battle took over the Cleveland Browns’ offseason and preseason. Now that the Browns are entering Week 5 with a...
articles.body:
Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders quarterback battle took over the Cleveland Browns' offseason and preseason. Now that the Browns are entering Week 5 with a 3-1 record after their 27-24 win against the Pittsburgh Steelers on October 1, many believe the Browns made a good call by going for veteran experience despite Watson not having played a full season since 2020.

But not everyone agrees that 2026 is Watson's comeback story.

"Dan, if you could separate the injuries from the off-field action, then yeah, it would be a comeback story," former Browns QB Robert Griffin III said on The Dan Patrick Show . "I just don't think you can do that. And you know, I've seen it feels like a lot of a lot of people are trying to do that," Griffin said. "And you know, I let my feelings be known about that years ago when the verdict was actually laid down. So it's not a comeback story."

Watson missed time in the last three seasons due to injuries. However, he was suspended for 11 games in the 2022 season following the NFL's investigation in light of the numerous sexual assault allegations against him. Watson came to Cleveland an already unpopular QB, and the team also drew flak for signing a player with such allegations against him.

The unpopularity only grew after Watson started missing more time in the subsequent seasons. He was out for the entirety of the 2025 season after he once again tore an already repaired Achilles in the preseason. 2026 was the last year on his contract with the Browns, which is worth $230 million. Many believe he hasn't done much to be given that much money.

This season was going to be do-or-die for him, and surprisingly, he's doing really well. The only way he could begin flipping the narrative was by winning games, and he's won three out of the four he's played so far. Deshaun Watson has thrown for 855 yards with an accuracy of an impressive 69.6%, along with six touchdowns through four games.

Though Griffin III may not be willing to believe it yet, Watson might be leaning into that redemption narrative now. During their matchup against the Steelers, he insisted that he walked out of the tunnel last. The fans, who booed him the first time he played at the Huntington Bank Field this preseason, welcomed him with a better response.

"I think the fans were a big part of that," Monken said. "And the reception he got as he came onto the field. Now, he earned that. But you have got to earn it. They weren't going to do that unless he'd earned it and where we were as a team. But I'm so happy for him, and we just started."

The Browns still have many more games to play this season, but it will define whether Deshaun Watson even gets to play next year or not. Whether or not that happens in Cleveland is left to be seen.

Shedeur Sanders had been the more popular quarterback this offseason, and many wanted him to start instead of Watson. FOX 8's Tino Bovenzi noted that there is still a bigger stock of Shedeur Sanders No. 2 jerseys compared to Watson's No. 4 in the Browns Pro Shop, and the veteran QB's jerseys are also highly discounted on the NFL shop's website.

But a fan told the network that if Watson begins to "rock," his jerseys will sell.

Is Deshaun Watson going to turn the tables this year? Only time will tell.

articles.title: Nick Sirianni or Jalen Hurts: Who Deserves More Blame for Eagles’ Offensive Collapse?
articles.summary: Sirianni and Hurts are facing criticism as Philadelphia's offense struggles. But who deserves more blame for the Eagles' recent collapse? Edit Snippet
articles.body:
The Philadelphia Eagles have a quarterback in Jalen Hurts making $51 million annually and a head coach, Nick Sirianni, with a Super Bowl championship on his résumé. Yet somehow, neither seems capable of figuring out how to move the football right now. Sirianni and Hurts have spent years proving critics wrong, but Philadelphia's latest performances are giving those same critics plenty of ammunition.

Seventeen consecutive failed third-down attempts. Just 27 points over two games. Those numbers would be embarrassing for a rebuilding team, let alone one with championship expectations.

Injuries have certainly contributed, but there's a legitimate argument over who should shoulder most of the blame, and it comes down to Sirianni and Hurts.

Hurts Isn't Playing Like a Franchise Quarterback

Jalen Hurts was awful against the Los Angeles Rams . There's no reason to sugarcoat it.

Twelve completions on 27 attempts for 93 yards . Philadelphia managed 172 total yards, which is difficult to accomplish with an NFL offense unless practically everything goes wrong.

Hurts certainly hasn't had much help. The Eagles are missing several important offensive players, including Lane Johnson, DeVonta Smith, and Saquon Barkley.

Still, that's what makes the criticism interesting. Is Hurts a quarterback who elevates the players around him, or does he need an exceptional supporting cast to be successful?

It's a question that's followed him for years.

Sirianni and Hurts won a championship together, but Hurts now has an opportunity to demonstrate that his value extends beyond the talent surrounding him.

He hasn't done much to settle that argument lately.

There were opportunities against Los Angeles to make plays, and Philadelphia's offense repeatedly failed to capitalize. Some of that comes down to protection, but Hurts can't escape responsibility for his own decisions.

When a quarterback commands that kind of salary, expectations don't disappear simply because a few starters are unavailable.

Sirianni Can't Keep Pointing to Injuries

Sirianni deserves credit for navigating Philadelphia through previous difficult stretches. His team looked finished at various points in 2024 before eventually winning the Super Bowl.

But past accomplishments don't explain what's happening now.

Sean Mannion is calling plays, and Philadelphia's offense has become painfully predictable. The Eagles went 0-for-12 on third down against Los Angeles. At some point, someone has to recognize that whatever they're trying isn't working.

That responsibility falls on the head coach.

Sirianni and Hurts have worked together long enough that the coaching staff should understand what the quarterback does well. Instead, Philadelphia looks like an offense trying to figure out its identity during the regular season.

Hurts can miss a throw or make a poor decision. Sirianni is responsible for ensuring those mistakes don't become part of a larger pattern.

Philadelphia has changed coordinators and shuffled personnel, yet the same questions keep coming up. Why does the offense struggle to adjust when its initial approach fails? Why do opposing defenses seem capable of dictating how the Eagles operate?

Those questions extend beyond Sirianni and Hurts.

Philadelphia's Problems Go Beyond Sirianni and Hurts

The injuries are real. Johnson's retirement, Cam Jurgens' departure, and the absence of other offensive contributors have forced Philadelphia to make significant adjustments. Unfortunately, the blame goes beyond just Sirianni and Hurts.

Nobody should expect the Eagles to look identical to their championship team. But asking them to convert an occasional third down doesn't seem unreasonable.

Sirianni and Hurts have enough experience to make adjustments without waiting for every injured player to return.

The offensive line needs help. The quarterback needs better protection. The play-calling needs to account for both.

Those are coaching problems as much as personnel problems.

Philadelphia also needs to reconsider how much it's asking Hurts to do. If the protection isn't holding up, quicker throws and simpler reads could help establish some rhythm.

The Eagles don't need every offensive possession to produce a touchdown. They need to stop putting their defense back on the field after three plays.

Hurts deserves criticism for his recent performances. A franchise quarterback has to provide more than 93 passing yards when his team needs him.

But Sirianni deserves more of the blame.

He oversees the offense, approves the approach, and ultimately answers for the results. The Eagles shouldn't need a completely healthy roster just to sustain a drive.

Sirianni and Hurts have earned their reputations through years of success. Neither should lose that credibility because of two bad games.

However, Philadelphia's problems aren't limited to two poor afternoons. The inability to adjust offensively has become a recurring concern, and the current injuries have exposed just how dependent the team has been on its established stars.

Hurts needs to execute the plays. Sirianni needs to make sure they're worth executing.

And if Philadelphia continues struggling, the head coach will have a much harder time explaining why nothing has changed.

articles.title: NFL picks: Who the experts predict to win in the Broncos-Chargers game
articles.summary: Who do the NFL experts think will win when the Los Angeles Chargers host the Denver Broncos? Here are their picks.
articles.body:
The Denver Broncos (2-2) don't want to become the first team to drop a game to the Los Angeles Chargers (0-4) this season, but they will need a full-team effort in order to accomplish that. Jim Harbaugh and Justin Herbert will be doing everything they can to prevent an 0-5 start. No team has ever started a season 0-5 and still made the playoffs.

In many ways, the Broncos could hand their division rivals an early-season knockout blow.

In order for that to happen, Bo Nix will need to step his game up and the Broncos will need to find something in the running game. Perhaps the switch back to Sean Payton as the offensive playcaller can improve that.

How do the experts see this one going? Do the Broncos send the Chargers to 0-5 or do the Chargers get their first win and drop the Broncos to 2-3?

Broncos vs. Chargers Week 5 expert picks

Jeremy Cluff, The Arizona Republic: Broncos 21, Chargers 17

"The Los Angeles Chargers can't fall to 0-5, can they? Yes, they can. Bo Nix will outduel Justin Herbert, and Denver will beat the Bolts at SoFi Stadium to move the Broncos to 3-2."

Pete Prisco, CBS Sports: Chargers 23, Broncos 17

"The Broncos are playing consecutive road games after losing at San Francisco last week," Prisco wrote for CBS. "The Chargers haven't won. They will here. Desperation will be in play for the Chargers. The Broncos have offensive issues right now that will show up. Look for Los Angeles to quiet the critics for a week."

Bill Bender, The Sporting News: Broncos 23, Chargers 20

"The Chargers are a desperate home underdog looking to turn a corner with Mike McDaniel and Jim Harbaugh," wrote Bender for The Sporting News. "The Broncos have struggled to run the football, which means Bo Nix will have to make enough plays on the road. Los Angeles has been called for 20 penalties on the offensive line this season – most in the NFL – and faces a daunting task against the Broncos' defensive front. The Chargers also are 0-4 ATS. We can't quite pull the upset here."

Bobby Kownack, NFL.com: Broncos 21, Chargers 17

"A lot of the elements that could've rendered this a precarious matchup for the Broncos are balanced out by the Chargers dealing with similar issues," wrote Kownack for NFL.com. "Denver has scored only 13 first-half points through four games, requiring a pair of comebacks from double-digit deficits just to be sitting at 2-2. Unless Sean Payton taking over the play-calling from first-year offensive coordinator Davis Webb drastically changes those early-game woes, the Broncos will remain vulnerable to opponents jumping out to sizeable leads. Luckily for Denver, the Chargers haven't proven to be capable of doing that thus far. They only cracked the 20-point mark for the first time last week. The Broncos could also be without their two top cornerbacks, Patrick Surtain II (ankle) and Riley Moss (rib), but Los Angeles will be dealing with absences at both offensive tackle spots; Joe Alt (neck) and Rashawn Slater (ankle) are both set to miss the contest. As long as Denver manufactures pressure against Justin Herbert, who has experienced a nightmare start to the campaign, the defense should be able to make life easier on its corners stepping into expanded roles. With this being a divisional matchup, the result could still end up closer than the records -- and general vibes -- suggest, but that's technically another point in the Broncos' favor. They tend to wake up and thrive in the clutch."
